title: Commutes Sentence of Charles Tanner
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Charles Tanner as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s commutation index lists Charles Tanner, convicted in the Northern District of Indiana of conspiring and attempting to possess at least five kilograms of cocaine for distribution. The record states that his sentence was 360 months’ imprisonment, as amended, plus ten years of supervised release and a $1,000 fine. Trump commuted his sentence on October 21, 2020.

title: Advocates file Nathan challenge to Trump's revised birthright order
description_short: Advocates file Nathan challenge to Trump's revised birthright order
description_medium: On September 28, 2026, immigrant-rights groups filed Nathan v. Trump in federal district court in Washington, D.C., challenging the administration’s revised birthright-citizenship order. The complaint seeks relief for children affected by the policy and alleges constitutional and statutory violations. The groups had first tried to raise the challenge in an earlier case, but filed a separate suit after the judge indicated it was a new legal challenge. No ruling on the complaint is described in the supplied reports.
description_long: Immigrant-rights organizations filed Nathan v. Trump on September 28, 2026, challenging President Trump’s August birthright-citizenship executive order. The plaintiffs’ groups include the American Civil Liberties Union and several state ACLU affiliates, the Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus and Democracy Defenders Fund. They brought the case on behalf of people subject to the revised order and seek relief for children who would be excluded from citizenship under the policy. The complaint alleges that the order violates constitutional and statutory protections; those are the plaintiffs’ claims, not a court’s ruling. The litigation followed a separate challenge to Trump’s earlier order. The groups had initially asked to block the revised order in Trump v. Barbara, but withdrew that request after the judge indicated the new policy required a separate lawsuit. They then filed Nathan in federal district court in Washington, D.C. The ACLU’s release says the Supreme Court had ruled in June in the Barbara case, and the groups relied on that decision in opposing the revised order. The available report describes the filing and requested relief, not a decision on the merits or the lawsuit’s eventual outcome.
